summary: Describes a mechanism for forwarding multicast based only on IGMP or MLD group membership information. In simple topologies, a device need not run a multicast routing protocol; it can learn membership and proxy it upstream. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: IGMP and MLD are how a computer tells the nearest router that it wants to receive a multicast group. This RFC describes a proxy device that uses only that information to forward multicast packets: it asks the subscribers what they want, tells the router above it what the total demand is, and copies each packet to the links that asked for it. It works only on a simple tree of devices.

questions: how does igmp proxy forwarding work
subtitle: Forwarding multicast packets with membership information alone, on a tree of proxy devices.

tldr.problem: A device that sits between a group of subscribers and the wider multicast network does not always need to run a multicast routing protocol to forward multicast traffic.
tldr.mechanism: A proxy device runs the router part of IGMP or MLD on its downstream interfaces and the host part on its upstream interface, merges what the subscribers asked for into one membership database, and forwards packets to the interfaces that asked for them and on which it is the querier.
tldr.outcome: The RFC limits the method to a manually configured tree in a single administrative domain, and it does not detect upstream loops, which must be ruled out administratively.

today: RFC 4605 is a Proposed Standard on the Internet standards track, and no RFC in the site index obsoletes or updates it. It describes a forwarding method for use inside one administrative domain and refers the reader to PIM and other multicast routing protocols for anything more complicated.

sections.title: Why Proxying Instead of Multicast Routing
sections.content:
This document applies spanning tree multicast routing to an environment that has only IGMP or MLD. The topology is limited to a tree, because the document specifies no protocol to build a spanning tree over a more complex topology. The root of the tree is assumed to be connected to a wider multicast infrastructure.

In a simple tree topology it is not necessary to run a multicast routing protocol at all. It is enough to learn and proxy group membership information and forward multicast packets on the strength of it. A typical example is an edge aggregation box such as a Digital Subscriber Line Access Multiplexer, which in most deployments has one connection to the core network and many connections to the customer side.

Using IGMP/MLD-based forwarding to replicate multicast traffic on such devices simplifies their design and implementation. By not supporting more complicated multicast routing protocols such as Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) or the Distance Vector Multicast Routing Protocol (DVMRP), it reduces the cost of the devices and the operational overhead. It also makes the proxy devices independent of the multicast routing protocol used by the core network routers, so they can be deployed in any multicast network.

Robustness in an edge box is usually achieved with a hot spare connection to the core network: when the first connection fails, the edge box fails over to the second. IGMP/MLD-based forwarding benefits from that, because the proxy upstream connection can be updated to the new connection at the same time.
sections.plainLanguage: Some devices sit between subscribers and the rest of the network and only need to pass multicast traffic along. Running a full multicast routing protocol on them is expensive, both to build and to operate. This RFC lets them work from the group subscriptions alone.

sections.title: Where This Applies
sections.content:
The IGMP/MLD-based forwarding only works in a simple tree topology. The tree must be manually configured by designating upstream and downstream interfaces on each proxy device. The IP addressing scheme applied to the proxying tree SHOULD also be configured so that a proxy device can win the IGMP/MLD Querier election and so be able to forward multicast traffic.

There are no other multicast routers inside the tree apart from the proxy devices, and the root of the tree is expected to be connected to a wider multicast infrastructure. The protocol is limited to a single administrative domain.

In more complicated scenarios, where the topology is not a tree, where a more robust failover mechanism is wanted, or where more than one administrative domain is involved, the RFC says a multicast routing protocol should be used instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The method needs a tree, configured by hand, inside one organisation. If the network is more complicated than that, or spans several organisations, use a real multicast routing protocol.

sections.title: Terms Used in This Document
sections.content:
An upstream interface is a proxy device's interface in the direction of the root of the tree, also called the host interface. Each of a proxy device's other interfaces is a downstream interface, also called a router interface.

A group is said to be in a particular group mode depending on which version of the protocol the reports use. In IPv4 environments, a group is in IGMP version 1 mode if an IGMPv1 report is heard, in IGMP version 2 mode if an IGMPv2 report is heard but no IGMPv1 report is heard, and in IGMP version 3 mode if an IGMPv3 report is heard but no IGMPv1 or IGMPv2 report is heard. In IPv6 environments the same pattern applies to MLD version 1 and version 2, with MLDv1 equivalent to IGMPv2 and MLDv2 equivalent to IGMPv3.

A subscription depends on the mode. When a group is in IGMPv1 or IGMPv2/MLDv1 mode, the subscription is a group membership on an interface. When a group is in IGMPv3/MLDv2 mode, the subscription is a state entry, a tuple of multicast address, group timer, filter mode and source-element list, on an interface.

The membership database is the database kept at each proxy device into which the membership information of each of its downstream interfaces is merged. It holds membership records of the form (multicast-address, filter-mode, source-list).
sections.plainLanguage: Each proxy device has one interface facing the root of the tree and one or more facing the subscribers. A subscription is either a simple yes, I want this group, or, in the newest version of the protocols, a record that also says which sources are wanted.

sections.title: The Abstract Protocol
sections.content:
A proxy device performing IGMP/MLD-based forwarding has a single upstream interface and one or more downstream interfaces. These designations are explicitly configured; there is no protocol to determine what type each interface is. The device performs the router portion of IGMP or MLD on its downstream interfaces and the host portion on its upstream interface, and it MUST NOT perform the router portion on the upstream interface.

The proxy device maintains a database consisting of the merger of all subscriptions on any downstream interface. It sends IGMP/MLD membership reports on the upstream interface when queried, and sends unsolicited reports or leaves when the database changes.

When the device receives a packet destined for a multicast group, which is a channel in Source-Specific Multicast, it builds a list consisting of the upstream interface and any downstream interface that has a subscription pertaining to that packet and on which it is the IGMP/MLD Querier. The list may be built dynamically or cached. It removes the interface on which the packet arrived and forwards the packet to the remaining interfaces, which may include the upstream interface.

The rule that a proxy device must be the querier in order to forward packets restricts the addressing scheme used. The devices must be given the lowest IP addresses of any potential IGMP/MLD Querier on the link, in order to win the election, and the election rule is that the querier with the lowest IP address wins. If a non-proxy device wins the election in an IGMP/MLD-based forwarding-only environment, no packets flow.

Electing a single forwarding proxy also avoids local loops and redundant traffic on links that several forwarders consider downstream. The RFC says this rule piggy-backs forwarder election on the querier election and delivers similar functionality on the local link to the PIM Assert mechanism. On a link with only one forwarding device the rule MAY be disabled, but the default configuration MUST include the querier rule, for example for redundancy.
sections.plainLanguage: On each subscriber link the proxy acts like a router and asks who wants what; on the link towards the root it acts like an ordinary subscriber and reports the total demand. A packet arriving is copied to the upstream link and to the downstream links that asked for it and where the proxy won the querier election.

sections.title: Topology Restrictions and Supporting Senders
sections.content:
The specification describes a protocol that works only in a simple tree topology. The tree must be manually configured by designating upstream and downstream interfaces on each proxy device, and the root of the tree is expected to be connected to a wider multicast infrastructure.

The election of a single forwarding proxy avoids local loops, but it does not protect against an upstream loop. In the RFC's example, device B forwards packets unconditionally from LAN 1 to LAN 2 and device A forwards unconditionally from LAN 2 to LAN 1, which causes an upstream loop. A multicast routing protocol that employs a tree building algorithm is required to resolve loops like this.

Senders inside the proxy tree need help from above. All traffic is forwarded towards the root, so the multicast routers connected to the wider multicast infrastructure should be configured to treat all systems inside the proxy tree as though they were directly connected. For Protocol Independent Multicast in Sparse Mode, for example, those routers should Register-encapsulate traffic from new sources within the proxy tree just as they would for directly connected sources. This information is likely to be configured by hand, because IGMP/MLD-based forwarding gives the routers upstream of the proxy tree no way to learn what networks are connected to it. If the proxy topology happens to match a routing topology, the information MAY instead be learned from the routing protocol running there.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rules keep the tree from looping traffic back and forth on the same link, but nothing stops two devices from forwarding traffic to each other along different links. That has to be prevented by hand, and the router above the tree has to be told to treat everything behind the tree as directly connected.

sections.title: The Membership Database
sections.content:
The proxy device performs the router portion of IGMP/MLD on each downstream interface. For each interface the version of IGMP/MLD used is explicitly configured and defaults to the highest version supported by the system. The output of that protocol is a set of subscriptions, maintained separately on each downstream interface, and the subscriptions on each downstream interface are merged into the membership database.

The membership database is a set of membership records of the form (multicast-address, filter-mode, source-list). Each record is the result of merging all subscriptions for that multicast address on the downstream interfaces. If some subscriptions are IGMPv1 or IGMPv2/MLDv1 subscriptions, they are converted to IGMPv3/MLDv2 subscriptions. The IGMPv3/MLDv2 subscriptions and the converted ones are first preprocessed to remove the timers, and, if the filter mode is EXCLUDE, to remove every source whose source timer is greater than zero. The preprocessed subscriptions are then merged using the merging rules for multiple memberships on a single interface from the IGMPv3 and MLDv2 specifications.

The RFC works through an example. Two downstream interfaces, I1 and I2, both have subscriptions for multicast address G. I1 has an IGMPv2/MLDv1 subscription that is (G). I2 has an IGMPv3/MLDv2 subscription with membership information (G, INCLUDE, (S1, S2)). The I1 subscription is converted to an IGMPv3/MLDv2 subscription with membership information (G, EXCLUDE, NULL), and the final membership record is (G, EXCLUDE, NULL).

On the upstream interface the proxy device performs the host portion of the protocol. If there is an IGMPv1 or IGMPv2/MLDv1 querier on the upstream network, the proxy device performs IGMPv1 or IGMPv2/MLDv1 accordingly, and otherwise it performs IGMPv3/MLDv2. When the composition of the membership database changes, the change is reported on the upstream interface as though the proxy device were a host performing the action. When the proxy device reports using IGMPv1 or IGMPv2/MLDv1, only the multicast address field in the membership record is used.
sections.plainLanguage: The proxy keeps one list of what the subscribers want, merged from all the subscriber links. Subscriptions from older versions of the protocol are rewritten into the newest form before merging, so the list always has the same shape.

sections.title: Forwarding Packets and Handling SSM
sections.content:
A proxy device forwards packets received on its upstream interface to each downstream interface, based on that interface's subscriptions and on whether the device is the IGMP/MLD Querier on it. It forwards packets received on any downstream interface to the upstream interface, and to each downstream interface other than the incoming one, on the same basis. It MAY use a forwarding cache instead of making this decision for each packet, but it MUST update the cache whenever any of the information used to build it changes.

To support Source-Specific Multicast (SSM), the proxy device should comply with the rules for using IGMPv3 for SSM. The RFC notes that it should comply with both the IGMP host requirement and the IGMP router requirement, because it performs the host portion on the upstream interface and the router portion on each downstream interface.

An interface can be configured to perform IGMPv1 or IGMPv2. In that case the SSM semantics are not maintained for that interface. A proxy device that supports this document should ignore IGMPv1 or IGMPv2 subscriptions sent to SSM addresses, and packets with source-specific addresses SHOULD NOT be forwarded to interfaces with IGMPv2 or IGMPv1 subscriptions for those addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Each arriving multicast packet is copied to the links that asked for that group, and to the link towards the root. With source-specific multicast, where a subscriber also names the sources it wants, the proxy follows the rules in RFC 4604 and keeps source-specific traffic away from older-style subscribers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Since only the querier forwards packets, the querier election may lead to black holes if a non-forwarder is elected querier. An attacker on a downstream LAN can cause itself to be elected querier, and as a result no packets would be forwarded.

There are operational ways to avoid this. It is fairly common for an operator to number the routers starting from the bottom of the subnet, so an operator SHOULD assign the subnet's lowest IP addresses to a proxy, or to proxies, in order for them to win the querier election.

IGMP/MLD-based forwarding does not provide the upstream loop detection mechanism described in section 3 of the RFC. To avoid the problems caused by an upstream loop, it MUST be administratively assured that such loops do not exist when deploying IGMP/MLD proxying.

The IGMP/MLD information presented by the proxy to its upstream routers is the aggregation of all its downstream group membership information. Any access control applied on the group membership protocol at the upstream router cannot be performed on a single subscriber, because the access control applies equally to all the interested hosts reachable via the proxy device.
sections.plainLanguage: The risk is that a device on a subscriber link wins the querier election, and then nothing is forwarded. Give the proxy the lowest address on the subnet to make that unlikely, and check by hand that the tree has no loops, because the protocol does not detect them itself.
